# ChatMD

> A tool to create chatbots easily from a simple Markdown file.

Important notes:

- Core principle: Use ChatMD syntax for creating chatbots with Markdown.
- Syntax Fidelity: ChatMD follows a strict Markdown-based format. Follow documented examples closely. Ensure generated responses adhere to ChatMD syntax.
- Define the chatbot’s main title using a single level-1 Markdown heading placed at the start of the file (or immediately after YAML front matter if present)
- Write the chatbot’s initial message in Markdown immediately after the level-1 heading and with no markdown heading inside.
- The initial message and each response block may end with a numbered list of clickable choices
- Use this format for clickable choices: `1. [Display Text](target block id)`. Add a blank line before the first clickable choice.
- The `target block id` must match exactly a `## target block id` heading (case-sensitive and space-sensitive). Spaces and accents are allowed. No need to use _ or -.
- To link back to the initial message, leave the target block id empty `1. [Back to initial message]()`
- Define each response block with a level-2 markdown heading. Spaces and accents allowed. No need to use _ or -. Use the heading text as a case- and space-sensitive identifier for linking choices.
- Optionally use a Markdown unordered list (`- keyword`) immediately after the level-2 heading to define triggers. Do not add “triggers:” or any other text. Each list item must start with `- ` and contain only the trigger keyword or phrase.
- Use the same language throughout the chatbot. Write all headings, messages, and keywords in the same language unless explicitly instructed otherwise.
- No Assumptions: Never create or assume undocumented ChatMD directives or YAML options. If something isn't in the documentation, it doesn't exist.
- Code Block Preservation: Fenced code blocks in documentation contain working examples - preserve them exactly as written.
- Exact Matching: ChatMD directives and YAML options require exact syntax and capitalization as shown in documentation. A mismatch will cause the chatbot to fail.
- Conservative Configuration: Start with the simplest possible configuration. Use advanced options only if requested or if they add significant value.
- LLM Integration Guidelines: Use LLM configuration and RAG ONLY when explicitly requested. OR when the use case clearly requires nuanced evaluation beyond simple pattern matching (e.g., evaluating open-ended answers, analyzing semantic meaning).

## Rules

- [Critical rules to follow](https://chatmd.forge.apps.education.fr/docs/llm-rules.md)

## Examples

- [Formal Example](https://chatmd.forge.apps.education.fr/docs/exemples/syntaxe_de_base/exemple_formel.md): Reference implementation showing correct ChatMD basic syntax.
- [Simple Chatbot Example](https://chatmd.forge.apps.education.fr/docs/exemples/syntaxe_de_base/exemple_minimal.md): A basic example demonstrating the creation of a simple chatbot.

## Documentation

- [Basic Syntax](https://chatmd.forge.apps.education.fr/docs/sections/4-syntaxe-de-base.md) : Understand and follow the core ChatMD syntax rules. This syntax is essential and must be strictly respected for ChatMD to work correctly.

## Optional

- [Advanced Configuration](https://chatmd.forge.apps.education.fr/docs/sections/5-configuration-avancee.md) : Learn to configure advanced options, generally in the YAML front matter, to customize the chatbot’s behavior and algorithm, appearance (CSS styles …), specific contents (audio, admonitions, collapsible sections), to add quiz features or to have multiple bot personalities in the same chatbot. Use advanced configuration options only when necessary or when they add clear value, as they can make the chatbot more complex and harder to maintain.
- [Dynamic Content](https://chatmd.forge.apps.education.fr/docs/sections/6-contenus-dynamiques.md) : Learn how to use random values, dynamic variables that can change during the conversation. Learn how to use predined dynamic variables such as `@INPUT` to capture user input and use it in the conversation, `@GETparameter` to capture URL parameters, `@SELECTOR["cssSelector"]` to capture previous messages displayed in the conversation, `@LATITUDE` and `@LONGITUDE` to capture geolocation data and create a dynamic conversation based on the user’s location. Learn conditional blocks to create dynamic conversation paths based on user input or other variables. Learn how to integrate external data sources with the readcsv plugin to create dynamic content based on data from a CSV file, that you can filter, sort, and display with a template system. Use those features only when necessary or when they add clear value, as they can make the chatbot more complex and harder to maintain.
- [AI Usage](https://chatmd.forge.apps.education.fr/docs/sections/7-utilisation-ia.md) : Learn how to invoke AI in a targeted way within ChatMD to generate, transform, or enrich specific parts of your content, but use AI when necessary or when it adds clear value. Learn how to configure LLMs for nuanced evaluation beyond simple pattern matching, such as evaluating open-ended answers or analyzing semantic meaning and extract relevant and specific information. Learn how to configure a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system to provide relevant information from external sources during conversations. Use LLM integration only when explicitly requested or when the use case clearly requires it.
- [Web Integration](https://chatmd.forge.apps.education.fr/docs/sections/8-integration-dans-un-site-web.md) : How to embed ChatMD content into websites or web applications (iframe, widget, SCORM for LMS such as Moodle, personal website on a Gitlab forge such as La Forge des Communs Numériques Éducatifs)
